question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old postmenopausal woman arrived to the surgical-oncology clinic for initial staging and medical clearance after an incidentally discovered 3.1-cm enhancing mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast was confirmed on core biopsy last week to be an invasive ductal carcinoma that appears confined to the breast parenchyma on diagnostic MRI and axillary ultrasound; she has not yet undergone lumpectomy, systemic therapy, or radiation and wishes to proceed with curative-intent surgery. She reports that the lesion was detected during her first mammogram in four years, obtained while being worked up for chronic fatigue, and she denies any weight loss, drenching night sweats, or bone pain. Her background medical history is notable for long-standing essential hypertension diagnosed in her late thirties, for which she takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and amlodipine 10 mg daily with home pressures usually in the 120s/70s; a renal sonogram performed two years ago showed bilaterally small echogenic kidneys without hydronephrosis, and serial metabolic panels have demonstrated a gradual rise in serum creatinine to 2.8 mg/dL today (baseline 2.6–2.9) corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 25 mL/min/1.73 m². She has never required dialysis, has no history of nephrolithiasis or obstructive uropathy, and spot urine protein measurements have remained in the sub-nephrotic range, leading her nephrologist to attribute the chronic kidney impairment to hypertensive nephrosclerosis rather than glomerular or diabetic pathology. Ten years ago she was found on routine laboratory screening to have fasting plasma glucose of 138 mg/dL, and since then she has managed her type 2 diabetes with diet, exercise, and metformin 1000 mg twice daily; her most recent hemoglobin A1c three months ago was 6.7 %, she denies visual changes, paresthesias of the feet, autonomic symptoms, or episodes of hypoglycemia, and slit-lamp examination last year showed no evidence of retinal microaneurysms, indicating absence of chronic microvascular sequelae. She emphatically denies any prior episodes of crushing substernal discomfort, diaphoresis with exertion, emergency department visits for chest pain, or cardiac catheterizations, and she has never been hospitalized for fluid overload, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, or lower-extremity edema suggestive of pump failure; her exercise tolerance remains adequate, as she walks her dog up a moderate hill daily without limitation apart from mild fatigue. She likewise denies calf claudication, nonhealing foot ulcers, prior vascular bypass grafts, transient monocular blindness, focal weakness, facial droop, slurred speech, or seizures, and her family confirms that her memory is sharp, she manages online banking, and there has been no personality change or repetitive questioning. She has never carried inhalers, does not cough chronically, has never been treated for bronchitis, and spirometry performed during a company physical two years ago showed a normal FEV1/FVC ratio. She drinks an occasional glass of wine on holidays, has never used illicit substances, and quit cigarettes at age 24 after a brief five-pack-year exposure. There is no history of abdominal pain relieved by food or antacids, hematemesis, melena, or prior endoscopic documentation of gastroduodenal ulceration. Viral hepatitis serologies obtained when her creatinine first began to rise were negative, liver-function tests have remained within reference intervals (AST 22 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 71 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, INR 1.0), and abdominal examination today demonstrates no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. She has never been told she has abnormal white blood cell clones, enlarged lymph nodes, or required chemotherapy for hematologic conditions, and HIV screening last year was nonreactive. Surgical history is limited to a vaginal hysterectomy for symptomatic fibroids at age 52 without complications. Current medications include lisinopril, amlodipine, metformin, low-dose aspirin for primary cardiovascular prophylaxis, cholecalciferol, and occasional acetaminophen for osteoarthritic knee discomfort; she takes no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, corticosteroids, or nephrotoxic herbal supplements. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fevers, chills, palpitations, syncope, dyspnea at rest, hemoptysis, abdominal distention, jaundice, easy bruising, dysuria, hematuria, or rash. On examination she is alert, oriented, and conversant, appearing her stated age and in no acute distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/72 mm Hg in the right arm seated, heart rate 76 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, body mass index 27 kg/m². Cardiovascular exam reveals a regular rhythm with crisp S1 and S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and jugular venous pulsation at 6 cm H₂O. Lungs are clear to auscultation with good air movement bilaterally. Abdomen is soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds and no palpable masses. Extremities show no edema, pulses are symmetric and 2+ in all distal vessels, and capillary refill is brisk. Neurologic evaluation demonstrates intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric strength and sensation, normal finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing, and a steady tandem gait. Skin inspection identifies a firm mobile nodule beneath the left areola corresponding to the imaging finding; no axillary or supraclavicular nodes are appreciated. Laboratory data from this morning show hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, platelets 238 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 46 mg/dL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL as noted, calcium 8.6 mg/dL, fasting glucose 118 mg/dL, and lipid profile with LDL 78 mg/dL. Electrocardiogram reveals normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min without Q waves, ST-T changes, or pathologic intervals. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed earlier this year for systolic murmur screening showed left ventricular ejection fraction 60 %, no regional wall-motion abnormalities, and trace mitral regurgitation only. She is seeking surgical removal of the localized breast carcinoma, and today’s visit documents her overall health status including well-controlled uncomplicated diabetes, advanced chronic kidney dysfunction attributed to longstanding hypertension, preserved cardiac and pulmonary function, intact cognition, no history of ischemic or hemorrhagic cerebrovascular events, absence of chronic gastrointestinal ulcer disease or hepatic compromise, and the lack of any prior systemic or hematologic malignancy or immunodeficiency.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weighted comorbidities present at assessment.
- Age 69 (60–69 years): 2 points.
- Active nonmetastatic solid tumor: biopsy-confirmed invasive breast carcinoma confined to the breast → 2 points.
- Moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease: sustained eGFR of 25 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates stage 4 CKD → 2 points.
- Uncomplicated diabetes: treated with metformin, without documented diabetic end-organ damage; the CKD is attributed to hypertension → 1 point.
- Hypertension is not a separate CCI item, and no other qualifying conditions are documented → 0 points.
Total = 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 7.
Final answer: 7
